summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applications. Trans and nonbinary travelers have reported passports confiscated or blocked, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; the policy is being challenged in federal courts.

Same-sex marriage remains contested on the ground. The Fono Senate voted down a bill to outlaw same-sex marriage in March 2003, and in 2015 American Samoa was the only US territory whose attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review. In January 2016 a newly confirmed District Court judge told the Senate he had not read Obergefell and that the court did not deal with it. A 2026 law review article by attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes Obergefell does apply and the territory would have to issue a certificate to any same-sex couple applying, while noting no couple has yet applied; a July 2024 on-island survey treats the local ban as operative and its constitutional durability as open.

Trans-specific violence and discrimination have produced federal legal action. In September 2023 the US Department of Justice settled an employment-discrimination case with the American Samoa Government over harassment of a transgender employee; a June 2023 federal civil action alleged a hostile work environment for a transgender woman suing the territorial government over her gender identity; and in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Local culture frames fa'afafine, defined as born male but embodying both male and female traits, as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture. The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa formed in 2010 on a cultural-pride footing. Reporting from 2009 described homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture, with reserved behaviour nonetheless expected under the fa'amatai chiefly system.
tangentialFactors:
American Samoa's position as a US territory means federal document and care policy applies directly, but its customary land and chiefly structures operate alongside territorial government, which shapes how protections are enforced in practice.

The territory's handling of same-sex marriage diverges from other US jurisdictions: Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply the 2015 federal ruling, while American Samoa's officials publicly questioned whether it applied. A 2026 legal analysis argues the ruling does apply regardless.

Contemporary reporting frames Samoan culture as comparatively accepting of homosexuality relative to other Pacific states such as Fiji, while also noting that reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations.
localsOnly:
Residents hold customary status through the fa'amatai chiefly system, and public conduct expectations under that system apply regardless of orientation.

Local advocacy is organised through the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS), formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, which anchors fa'afafine identity to cultural pride.

Territorial employment protections have been enforced federally: the US Department of Justice settlement with the American Samoa Government in September 2023 resolved an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and a June 2023 federal civil action alleged a hostile work environment for a transgender woman suing the territorial government.

A territorial same-sex marriage ban remains on the books and was treated as operative in a July 2024 on-island survey, even as a 2026 law review article argues the federal marriage ruling supersedes it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether a same-sex couple applying for a marriage licence in American Samoa would actually receive one is unresolved: a 2026 legal analysis says the territory would have to issue a certificate, but no application has been recorded to date.

The constitutional durability of the territorial same-sex marriage ban against a 14th Amendment challenge is an open question, with a July 2024 survey by a Miami University professor designed to test it; no court ruling resolving it is sourced here.

The outcome of the ACLU's suit against the State Department over passport sex markers, and the current posture of other federal court challenges to the January 2025 document policy, are unresolved in the sources.

Whether the federal employment-discrimination settlement and hostile-work-environment litigation produced lasting policy change within the American Samoa Government is not sourced.
